clue.text: Preferring not to be put in the picture

definitions.text: Preferring not to be put in the picture

blocks.note: surface reading: being told what is going on, briefed

blocks.clueFragment: Preferring not to be put in the picture
blocks.note: setter's reading: reluctant to appear in a photograph

explanation.surface: Someone who would rather not be told what is going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put in the picture' is an idiom for being informed; read literally it means being photographed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone shy of cameras dislikes being photographed, which is literally being placed inside a picture.

clue.text: Lost Owl and Pussycat found here?

blocks.note: first meaning: confused, bewildered
second meaning: in Edward Lear's poem the Owl and the Pussycat went to sea in a pea-green boat

explanation.surface: Where might the lost pair from the nursery poem turn up?
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Lear's nonsense poem begins 'The Owl and the Pussycat went to sea', so they would be found on the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: Being completely bewildered is idiomatically described as being out on the ocean, adrift without bearings.

clue.text: Ring to shed some light on Head of Religious Studies

definitions.text: shed some light on Head of Religious Studies

blocks.note: first meaning: to surround with a circle of light

blocks.clueFragment: shed some light on Head of Religious Studies
blocks.note: second meaning, cryptic: put a shining nimbus on the head of a saint, a figure studied in religion

explanation.surface: A call to explain things to the head of a school's RE department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of Religious Studies' sounds like a teacher, but it is the literal head of a holy figure, which a halo lights up.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to encircle with a halo, the luminous circle painted round a saint's head.

clue.text: See 9
Icarus had things so to raise levels of excitement

blocks.note: first meaning: Icarus flew close to the sun, where conditions were scorching aloft
second meaning: to intensify, become livelier

explanation.surface: The myth of Icarus used to stir up some excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: Icarus flew too near the sun and his wax wings melted: it was warm high in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to intensify or become livelier, as when a contest grows more thrilling.

clue.text: Game black lecturer stripped off to enthral raving mad Poles

indicators.note: raving suggests wild disorder, so the next word's letters are thrown into a new order
to enthral is to hold captive, so one piece holds the other inside it

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
L is the standard abbreviation for lecturer
naked is 'in the buff'
taken as written
the north and south poles, N and S

explanation.surface: A lecturer strips off to entertain some wild Polish visitors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the buff' is an idiom for naked; the setter drops 'the'. 'Poles' are the compass points, not people from Poland.
explanation.definitionFit: Blind man's buff is a children's party game in which a blindfolded player tries to catch the others.

clue.text: Ridiculous man excitedly beating boy around home

blocks.note: a man is a he
athrob means throbbing, pulsing with excitement
at home is in
a boy is a son

explanation.surface: A man is excitedly thrashing a boy somewhere near the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beating' is not a thrashing but a pulse; 'around' here means near, so the boy simply sits beside home.
explanation.definitionFit: William Heath Robinson drew absurdly elaborate contraptions, so his name is an adjective for ludicrously over-complicated devices.

clue.text: True indications Winchester will play Harrow and Eton Charterhouse?

definitions.text: Winchester will play Harrow and Eton Charterhouse?

blocks.note: first meaning: neckwear in a school's colours genuinely signals where the wearer was educated

blocks.clueFragment: Winchester will play Harrow and Eton Charterhouse?
blocks.note: second meaning, cryptic: drawn matches between long-established public schools

explanation.surface: A fixture list of matches between famous English public schools.
explanation.walkthrough: Winchester, Harrow, Eton and Charterhouse are old English public schools; a tie is also a match or a drawn result.
explanation.definitionFit: The striped neckwear of a former pupil marks their schooling, and fixtures between ancient schools are likewise matches of that kind.

clue.text: Dodgy “charitable” offer folk fly to?

annotation.answer: IT FELL OFF THE BACK OF A LORRY

blocks.note: surface reading: a suspicious gift offered as if out of kindness
setter's reading: the stock excuse a seller gives for cheap stolen goods, which buyers rush to snap up

explanation.surface: People flock to a suspiciously generous offer.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is the knowing British excuse for goods that are almost certainly stolen; 'charitable' hints it seems a giveaway.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying goods came that way is the classic euphemism for selling stolen merchandise cheaply, no questions asked.

clue.text: See 9
Number in outfit for party where one is assured of a friendly reception?

definitions.text: where one is assured of a friendly reception?

indicators.note: one item placed in another is being enclosed by it

blocks.note: the costume of a toga party
N is the abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: A costume for a fancy-dress party where guests are sure of a warm welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: Tonga is known as the Friendly Islands, the name Captain Cook gave it after a warm reception.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pacific kingdom's nickname, the Friendly Islands, makes it a place where visitors expect a hospitable welcome.

clue.text: Foremost of producers has desire to settle cast

indicators.note: foremost means the very front, so only the opening letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of producers
an itch is a restless desire

explanation.surface: A leading producer wants to finalise the casting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like actors, but it is the verb to throw; 'settle' also fits, as a bird pitches on a branch.
explanation.definitionFit: To pitch a ball is to throw or hurl it, the same action as casting a line or stone.

clue.text: The animal that emerges from monopoly players

indicators.note: something emerging from inside a phrase was already sitting within its letters

blocks.note: found across the two words

explanation.surface: A creature popping out of a Monopoly box during a game.
explanation.definitionFit: A polyp is a simple sessile sea creature such as a coral or sea anemone individual.

clue.text: London Recorder looks for Listener

indicators.note: for someone listening, the word is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: quick looks are peeps

explanation.surface: A London tape recorder is hunting for a listener.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Pepys, pronounced 'peeps', kept the famous diary of 1660s London; The Listener was also a magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: The seventeenth-century diarist chronicled London life, including the Great Fire and plague, making him the city's great chronicler.

clue.text: Vessel’s name taken from one in Joyce’s book?

indicators.note: taking something away from a word removes those letters from it

blocks.note: to dub is to name
James Joyce wrote the story collection Dubliners

explanation.surface: A ship named after a character in a James Joyce novel.
explanation.walkthrough: DUBLINER minus DUB leaves LINER.
explanation.definitionFit: A liner is a large passenger ship, a type of seagoing vessel.

clue.text: Contempt for mum kept in hand

indicators.note: kept in means held inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a paw is informal for a hand
mum means silent, as does the hushing sound

explanation.surface: Someone holds their mother's hand while feeling contempt for her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' is not mother but the word for keeping quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: Pshaw is an exclamation expressing disdain or impatient dismissal.

clue.text: Fur is whose? Elgar’s, I think

blocks.note: the hesitant noise of someone unsure
Elgar is the setter, so the setter answers 'whose?' with this possessive

explanation.surface: A dispute over who owns a fur coat, with the composer Elgar tentatively claiming it.
explanation.walkthrough: Elgar is the setter's pseudonym, so 'Elgar's' is the setter saying it belongs to him.
explanation.definitionFit: Ermine is the white winter coat of the stoat, prized as a luxurious pelt for robes.

clue.text: Sacred object taken to heart by 23 and 20

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so the outer letters of each referenced answer are discarded

blocks.note: the centre of the answer to 23, its first and last letters dropped
the central pair of letters of the answer to 20

explanation.surface: A holy relic that two other answers hold dear.
explanation.walkthrough: The hearts of ESCARP and ARABIC are taken, ignoring the outer letters of each.
explanation.definitionFit: The scarab beetle was sacred in ancient Egypt, and amulets carved in its shape were revered objects.

clue.text: Drink to which horse might lead you

definitions.text: to which horse might lead you

blocks.note: first meaning: a mixed drink of spirits and fruit juice

blocks.clueFragment: to which horse might lead you
blocks.note: second meaning, cryptic: the Suffolk ... is a breed of heavy horse

explanation.surface: A twist on leading a horse to water: here it leads you to a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: It plays on the proverb about leading a horse to water. The Suffolk Punch is a British draught-horse breed.
explanation.definitionFit: The bowl drink and the horse breed share the name, so thinking of horses can bring the word to mind.

clue.text: Fool standing in pasture’s shown clemency

indicators.note: standing in a field means being inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a ley is grassland or pasture
a nit is a fool

explanation.surface: A fool stood in a field and was shown mercy.
explanation.definitionFit: Lenity is mildness or mercifulness, an old word for gentle leniency in punishment.

clue.text: What are basic new air filters? Made in Saudi

indicators.note: new means freshly made, so the following letters are remade in another order
something that filters through seeps into the gaps of another thing

blocks.note: the ABC of a subject is its basics
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about basic air filters manufactured in Saudi Arabia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filters' pictures a device, but it is a verb: the jumbled letters seep into the gaps of the basics, two after the first letter and one after the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Something originating in Saudi Arabia is Arabian, and Arabic describes the language and culture of that region.

clue.text: Mackay or Barrowclough’s common salary?

blocks.note: first meaning: the two prison officers in the British sitcom Porridge, and a warder is slangily called this
second meaning: in slang, one's wages

explanation.surface: Asking about the ordinary pay of two named men.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Mackay and Mr Barrowclough are warders in Porridge, a 1970s BBC prison sitcom; 'common' marks slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Prison warders are slangily called screws, and the same word is old British slang for pay or wages.

clue.text: Chirpy individual, the Terry-Thomas type, captured by spies

indicators.note: someone captured is held inside, so one piece is surrounded by the other

blocks.note: the American intelligence agency
the actor Terry-Thomas played caddish bounders

explanation.surface: A cheerful bounder like Terry-Thomas is caught by secret agents.
explanation.walkthrough: Terry-Thomas was a British comic actor famous for playing gap-toothed cads.
explanation.definitionFit: The cicada is an insect noted for its loud chirping song, so it is literally chirpy.

clue.text: In a (less conventional) sense, vehicle goes down slope

indicators.note: one thing in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: extrasensory perception, an unconventional sixth sense
a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: In an unusual way, a vehicle heads down a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: ESP, extrasensory perception, is the 'sixth sense'.
explanation.definitionFit: An escarp is a steep bank or slope, especially one forming part of a fortification.

clue.text: Instance of lying on hay will supply it

definitions.note: a description of the answer rather than a synonym

blocks.note: a fib is a small lie
re means on or concerning

explanation.surface: Someone lying in a haystack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lying on hay' pictures a rest in a barn, but lying here is telling untruths.
explanation.definitionFit: Hay is coarse dried grass, rich in the roughage livestock need for digestion.

clue.text: The climax of the opening race?

indicators.note: a climax comes at the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: the last letter of the
a vent is an opening

explanation.surface: Asking about the thrilling finish of the first race of a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: A race is a single competition on a sports programme, which is called an event.

clue.text: Patriot rattling his sabre during the Beijing Olympics

indicators.note: during means within the span of something, so the word sits inside the phrase

blocks.note: found across the two words

explanation.surface: A nationalist brandishing his sword at the 2008 Beijing Games.
explanation.definitionFit: A jingo is an aggressively bellicose nationalist, the kind who threatens war at every opportunity.

clue.text: Pilgrim’s possessed, declining holy war

indicators.note: the part of the pilgrim meaning possessed goes into decline, sinking to the bottom of this down light

blocks.note: a hadji is a Muslim who has made the pilgrimage to Mecca

explanation.surface: A pilgrim, gripped by something, refuses to fight a holy war.
explanation.walkthrough: HADJI begins with HAD (possessed); that chunk drops to the foot to give JI + HAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Jihad is an Arabic term for a struggle, popularly a religious war fought in defence of Islam.

clue.text: Actively seeking rage to some extent?

blocks.note: to be after something is to pursue it
a rage, as in 'all the rage', is a craze or vogue

explanation.surface: Someone angrily pursuing something, but only partly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rage' looks like anger, but it is the vogue sense, as in all the rage.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means in a rough or imperfect way, done only partially or after some fashion.

clue.text: In past, drop with a jerk

definitions.text: In past, drop with a jerk

indicators.note: a jerk is a sudden violent jolt, which throws the words into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A description of an old punishment involving a sudden fall stopped short.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the torture, used in the past, of hoisting a victim by the wrists and letting them fall.
explanation.definitionFit: The strappado was a historical torture in which a bound prisoner was dropped and halted abruptly by a rope.
